topics.title: Matter and its properties
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
topics.concept: Chemistry studies matter (anything that has mass and occupies space) and its changes. Matter exists as solid, liquid or gas; properties are physical or chemical; pure substances have fixed composition while mixtures are separated by physical methods.

subtopics.title: Chemistry and its branches
subtopics.concept: Main branches: organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, biochemistry, industrial and nuclear chemistry.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_refs.section: Introduction – branches of chemistry; chemistry and industry

subtopics.title: States of matter and changes of state
subtopics.concept: Solids: particles closely packed, vibrate about fixed positions; liquids: particles close but free to slide; gases: particles far apart, moving freely. Melting point = solid → liquid; freezing, evaporation, condensation, sublimation.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

subtopics.title: What is matter; physical and chemical properties
subtopics.concept: Matter has mass and occupies space (gold, CO, steam, brass); heat, light and sound are forms of energy, not matter. Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts (silver does not react with dilute HCl); physical properties are observed without changing the substance (softness, lustre, conductivity, solubility).

subtopics.title: Separating mixtures
subtopics.concept: Physical methods based on differences in physical properties: filtration, evaporation, distillation, fractional distillation, sublimation, magnetic separation, chromatography, separating funnel (immiscible liquids such as oil and water – the less dense oil forms the upper layer).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

topics.title: Atomic structure, symbols, formulas and the mole
topics.concept: Atoms contain a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in shells. Symbols, formulas and names follow fixed rules; the mole links mass to number of particles.

subtopics.title: Protons, neutrons, electrons; isotopes
subtopics.concept: Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons; in an ion, electrons = Z − charge. Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

subtopics.title: Electron configuration, valence electrons and isoelectronic species
subtopics.concept: Maximum electrons in shell n = 2n² (4th shell 32). Ar: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. Elements of the same group have the same number of valence electrons (Na, K: 1). Isoelectronic species have equal numbers of electrons (O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Mg²⁺: 10).

subtopics.title: Symbols, formulas and names
subtopics.concept: Some symbols come from Latin names: Na (natrium), K (kalium), Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Sn, Sb, Hg, Pb. -ate / -ite anions: MgSO₄ magnesium sulphate, MgSO₃ magnesium sulphite. The salt of H₃PO₄ with K⁺ is K₃PO₄.

subtopics.title: The mole, percentage composition and empirical formula
subtopics.concept: n = mass ÷ molar mass; number of particles = n × 6.02×10²³. Percentage composition = mass of element ÷ formula mass × 100. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio; it equals the molecular formula when the subscripts have no common factor (CH₄).

subtopics.title: Types of chemical reactions
subtopics.concept: Combination, decomposition, single replacement (a more active element replaces a less active one: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂), double replacement and combustion.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.concept: Early classifications (Döbereiner's triads, Newlands' octaves, Mendeleev) used atomic mass; the modern table is arranged by atomic number. Metallic and non-metallic character, radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity change periodically.

subtopics.title: Historical classification and groups
subtopics.concept: Döbereiner (1829) grouped similar elements in triads arranged by increasing atomic mass (middle mass ≈ average of the other two). Group IA = alkali metals, IIA = alkaline earth metals, VIIA = halogens, VIIIA/0 = noble gases.

textbook_refs.section: 1.2 The modern periodic table – periods and groups
1.2 Groups of the periodic table – halogens

subtopics.title: Properties of metals and non-metals
subtopics.concept: Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors; graphite is the non-metal that conducts; diamond does not conduct electricity.

topics.title: Chemical bonding and intermolecular forces
topics.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
topics.concept: Intramolecular forces (ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent, metallic bonds) hold atoms together; intermolecular forces (dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonds, ion–dipole) act between molecules.

subtopics.title: Intramolecular bonds versus intermolecular forces
subtopics.concept: Ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds are intramolecular. Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force. Polar HCl molecules attract each other by dipole–dipole forces.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

topics.title: Solutions
topics.concept: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures; they are classified by state and by degree of saturation. Concentration is given as mass percent, molarity or normality; solubility depends on temperature, pressure and 'like dissolves like'; colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles.

subtopics.title: Solutions; saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated
subtopics.concept: All solutions are homogeneous mixtures (solid, liquid or gas). A supersaturated solution holds more solute than a saturated one; a seed crystal makes the excess crystallise, so the crystal grows.

subtopics.title: Mass percent, molarity and normality
subtopics.concept: Molarity = moles of solute per litre of solution, so equal molarities mean equal moles per litre (not equal masses).

subtopics.title: Solubility and factors affecting it
subtopics.concept: Solubility = amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. Like dissolves like (polar/ionic in water, non-polar in non-polar solvents). Gas solubility increases with lower temperature and higher pressure. Dissolving happens when solute–solvent attractions can overcome solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions. Sodium, potassium, ammonium salts and nitrates are soluble; CaCO₃, BaSO₄ are insoluble.

textbook_refs.section: 3.3.1 Solubility of solutes in liquids – like dissolves like

subtopics.title: Colligative properties
subtopics.concept: Vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on the number of solute particles – colour and solubility are not colligative.

topics.title: Acids, bases and salts
topics.concept: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red and donate protons; bases taste bitter, feel slippery, turn red litmus blue and accept protons. Strong acids and bases ionise completely, weak ones only slightly. pH is estimated with indicators.

subtopics.title: Properties, strength and definitions of acids and bases
subtopics.concept: Acids: sour, H⁺/H₃O⁺ producers, turn blue litmus red. Bases: bitter, slippery, turn red litmus blue, neutralise acids. Weak acids (CH₃COOH) and weak bases (NH₃) ionise slightly. Diprotic acids have two acidic H (H₂SO₄, H₂CO₃). pH is estimated with indicators or pH paper.

textbook_refs.section: 4.1.4 Chemical properties of acids – reaction with carbonates

subtopics.title: Preparation of acids, bases and salts
subtopics.concept: Acids: non-metal oxide + water, direct combination of elements (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl). Bases: very active metal + water (2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂), metal oxide + water, salt + base. Salts contain the metal cation and the acid's anion (H₃PO₄ → K₃PO₄).

topics.title: Energy and chemical reactions
topics.concept: Kinetic energy (thermal, electrical) is energy of motion of particles; potential energy (chemical) is stored. Heat flows from hot to cold. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH > 0).

subtopics.title: Forms of energy, transformations and heat flow
subtopics.concept: Energy due to the motion of particles is kinetic energy. Photosynthesis changes light energy into chemical energy. Heat is the most common form of energy change in reactions. Heat flows from the hotter body to the colder one (body → cold bench).

textbook_refs.section: 5.1 Energy transformations (Activity: plant, candle, light bulb)

subtopics.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions and energy diagrams
subtopics.concept: Exothermic: heat is a product, ΔH negative (combustion, freezing, condensation). Endothermic: heat absorbed, ΔH positive (photosynthesis, melting). On an energy diagram ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants); Ea is from reactants to the peak.

textbook_refs.section: 5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions; 5.2 energy diagrams

topics.title: Chemical equilibrium
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
topics.concept: Reversible reactions reach dynamic equilibrium; Le Chatelier's principle predicts how a system at equilibrium responds to a change in concentration, pressure/volume or temperature.

subtopics.title: Measuring rates of reaction
subtopics.concept: The rate of a reaction is followed by measuring a property that changes with time: volume of gas evolved, loss or gain of mass, colour, pH, temperature or conductivity.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
textbook_refs.section: 1.1.1 Measuring the rate of a chemical reaction

subtopics.title: Reaction quotient Q and equilibrium constant K
subtopics.concept: Q has the same form as K but uses any concentrations. Q < K: too few products, net reaction goes right. Q > K: too many products, net reaction goes left. Q = K: at equilibrium.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it

topics.title: Oxidation–reduction and electrolysis
topics.concept: Oxidation = addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number. Electrolysis uses a DC source, electrodes and an electrolyte; Q = I × t.

subtopics.title: Oxidation and reduction
subtopics.concept: Addition of oxygen (S + O₂ → SO₂) is oxidation; gain of electrons (Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻) is reduction.

textbook_refs.section: 2.1 Oxidation and reduction; oxidizing and reducing agents

subtopics.title: Electrolytes and electrolysis
subtopics.concept: Strong electrolytes dissociate completely into ions; weak ones partially. An electrolytic cell needs a DC source, anode, cathode and electrolyte (an ammeter or bulb shows the current). Quantity of electricity Q = I × t (A × s = C).

textbook_refs.section: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis – purification of copper

topics.title: Nonmetals and their compounds
topics.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Carbon (allotropes, amorphous forms, CO₂ and the carbon cycle), nitrogen (ammonia, Haber process) and sulphur compounds (sulphuric acid by the Contact process).

subtopics.title: Carbon: allotropes, amorphous forms and carbon dioxide
subtopics.concept: Crystalline allotropes: diamond (non-conductor), graphite (conductor), fullerene. Amorphous forms: coke, wood charcoal, animal charcoal, carbon black. Burning fuels and deforestation raise atmospheric CO₂; planting trees removes CO₂ by photosynthesis.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

subtopics.title: Ammonia and the Haber process
subtopics.concept: Ammonia is colourless, has a choking/pungent smell, is lighter than air, very soluble and forms a weakly alkaline solution. Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: controlled by temperature, pressure, concentration and an iron catalyst.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

subtopics.title: Sulphur: occurrence and allotropes
subtopics.concept: Sulphur occurs free (Marsa Fatuma, Erta Ale) and as pyrite FeS₂, ZnS, CuFeS₂ and CuS in Eritrea (Debarwa, Adi Nefas). Allotropes: rhombic (stable below 96 °C, octahedral crystals) and monoclinic (stable above 96 °C, needle-shaped).

Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

subtopics.title: Carbon monoxide and gaseous fuels
subtopics.concept: Water gas = CO + H₂ (steam over hot coke); producer gas = CO + N₂. CO is a reducing agent in metal extraction.

topics.title: Metals and metallurgy
topics.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Metals have high melting and boiling points and conduct electricity. Reactivity with air, water and acids follows the activity series. Metallurgy: concentration, roasting/calcination, reduction and refining.

subtopics.title: Activity series and reactions of metals
subtopics.concept: K, Na, Ca react with cold water (K most vigorously); Mg with hot water; Zn, Fe with steam; Pb, Cu, Ag, Au do not. Metals above hydrogen (Zn) displace H₂ from dilute acids; Cu, Ag, Au do not. With air: Na, K very reactive; Fe, Zn moderately; Au, Pt unreactive.

subtopics.title: Properties of metals, corrosion and extraction
subtopics.concept: Metals generally have high melting and boiling points. Copper corrodes in moist air. Carbonate ores are converted to oxides by calcination; very active metals (K, Na, Ca) are obtained by electrolysis.

topics.title: Behaviour of gases
topics.concept: Gas laws: Boyle (P ∝ 1/V), Charles (V ∝ T), Gay-Lussac (P ∝ T at constant V), combined gas law. STP = 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm. Kinetic theory explains pressure by molecular collisions.

subtopics.title: Gas laws and standard conditions
subtopics.concept: At constant volume P ∝ T (kelvin): P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂. At constant pressure V ∝ T. Standard temperature is exactly 0 °C = 273.15 K.

textbook_refs.section: 5.2.3 Avogadro's law; 5.2.5 The ideal gas law

subtopics.title: Kinetic molecular theory of gases
subtopics.concept: Pressure comes from molecular collisions with the walls; raising the temperature makes molecules move faster, so collisions become more frequent and forceful and pressure rises.

textbook_refs.section: 5.3 Kinetic molecular theory; real and ideal gases

topics.title: Shapes of molecules and crystals
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
topics.concept: VSEPR predicts electron-pair and molecular geometries; solids are crystalline or amorphous; crystals are described by lattices, unit cells and crystal systems.

subtopics.title: VSEPR shapes and bond angles
subtopics.concept: Linear 180°, trigonal planar 120°, tetrahedral 109.5° (CH₄).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

subtopics.title: Crystals, lattices, unit cells and crystal systems
subtopics.concept: A crystal (crystalline solid) has atoms, ions or molecules arranged in an orderly repeating pattern; the crystal lattice is the pattern, the unit cell the repeating unit. Cubic unit cell: a = b = c, all axial angles 90°.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

topics.title: Organic chemistry
topics.concept: Organic compounds are compounds of carbon (except CO, CO₂, carbonates). Hydrocarbons contain only C and H; alkenes undergo addition reactions; functional groups (alcohols, acids, esters) and polymers.

subtopics.title: Addition reactions of alkenes
subtopics.concept: Hydrogenation (+H₂), halogenation (+X₂) and hydrohalogenation (+HX: HCl, HBr, HI) of alkenes.

subtopics.title: Functional groups and esterification
subtopics.concept: Carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water (esterification, acid catalyst).

subtopics.title: Homologous series and IUPAC naming
subtopics.concept: Members of a homologous series share a general formula (alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) and a functional group and differ by CH₂. Alkyl groups CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ (methyl, ethyl) are side branches. Name from the longest chain and number to give the functional group the lowest locant.

topics.title: Nuclear chemistry
topics.concept: Nuclear reactions change the nucleus and can convert one element into another; stability depends on the neutron-to-proton ratio. Fission splits heavy nuclei (atomic bomb); fusion joins light nuclei (hydrogen bomb, Sun).

subtopics.title: Nuclear reactions and stability
subtopics.concept: Only nuclear reactions convert atoms of one element into another (transmutation). The main factor in nuclear stability is the n/p ratio.

subtopics.title: Nuclear fission and fusion
subtopics.concept: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits (atomic bomb, reactors). Fusion: light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes fuse (hydrogen bomb, the Sun).
